newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan leaders expect better ties with U.S..
newsitem.headline: Pakistan leaders expect better ties with U.S..

text.p: Pakistan government leaders, facing turmoil after the sacking of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, on Thursday hailed U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election and voiced hopes he would take an active political role in the region.

President Farooq Leghari and the new caretaker Prime Minister Meraj Khalid both sent warm messages to Clinton, whose text were issued by government, after an earlier subdued greeting by a Foreign Ministry spokesman compared to an enthusiastic statement by Bhutto a day earlier.

The spokesman said Pakistan hoped Clinton would take up a promised initiative to settle political problems in South Asia, notably the long-standing dispute between Pakistan and India over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.

"We value and appreciate your foreign policy initiatives, specially in our part of the world," Leghari's message said. "These have restored and strengthened the confidence and trust of long-standing friends like Pakistan."

Khalid, named caretaker prime minister to supervise fresh elections in early February, said he looked forward to working with the Clinton administration "to cement our relationship", uphold democratic principles, enhance economic cooperation, promote nuclear non-proliferation and strengthen global and regional stability.

The Foreign Ministry spokesman said Islamabad had also noted with satisfaction that several U.S. Congressmen friendly to Pakistan had also been re-elected, and Senator Larry Pressler, considered hostile to Pakistan, had lost the re-election bid.
Pressler had authored legislation that led to a cutoff of U.S. military aid to Pakistan.

The spokesman recalled that Clinton had said in a campaign statement he would take an initiative towards settling political problems in South Asia, where arch-foes India and Pakistan have a longstanding dispute over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
"We will look forward to such an initiative by the new administration of the United States," the spokesman said.
Washington has offered to mediate between India and Pakistan over Kashmir if both countries agreed, a suggestion welcomed by Islamabad but firmly rejected by India.

Pakistan's official comment appeared lukewarm compared to that of Bhutto, who on Wednesday enthusiastically greeted Clinton's re-election, saying he was "the perfect person" to lead the United States into the 21st century.
Leghari sacked Bhutto's three-year-old government on Tuesday, dissolved the National Assembly and named the caretaker prime minister to supervise elections on February 3.
